young.html: Besides plays, Shakespeare wrote 154 short poems called sonnets. Every sonnet has exactly fourteen lines, and every line has a steady beat of ten syllables: da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM.

The most famous one begins by asking whether the person he loves is like a summer's day. His answer: no, you are even better, because summer ends but you will live forever in this poem. And here we are, four hundred years later, still reading it!

young.html: Write a mini-sonnet. A real sonnet is hard, so try the last two lines, the couplet. Write two lines of about ten syllables that rhyme, about someone or something you love. ("My dog is old and slow and fond of naps, / But no one greets me better at the door." Oops, that doesn't rhyme. Try again!)

full.html: Shake-speares Sonnets was published in 1609, probably without much help from the poet. It holds 154 sonnets and a longer poem, A Lover's Complaint. Many of the sonnets were likely written in the 1590s, when sonnet sequences were the fashion in England.

head: Sonnets
Mostly about
rows: Urging a beautiful young man to marry and have children, so his beauty will live on
Love for the young man, time, absence, jealousy, and poetry's power to last
A "dark lady" the poet loves against his own judgment
full.cap: The usual grouping. Who the young man and the lady were is unknown and much debated.

full.html: The sonnet came from Italy, where Petrarch (1300s) made it famous: eight lines, then six. English poets reshaped it into the form now named for Shakespeare: three quatrains (groups of four lines) and a closing couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in iambic pentameter. Often the poem makes a turn (the volta) at line 9, and the couplet sums up or twists the argument.

full.name: gb-sonnet
full.cap: Switch between Sonnet 18 and Sonnet 116, and between the rhymes and the four parts.

full.text:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date:
...
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: Lines 1–4 and 9–14. "Ow'st" means own; "fair," beauty. Spelling as in the Project Gutenberg text.

full.html: The poem's boast is that verse outlasts time: the beloved will live "in eternal lines." The "lines" are both lines of verse and, perhaps, lines of descent.

full.text:
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:
O, no! it is an ever-fixed mark,
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wandering bark,
Whose worth's unknown, although his height be taken.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: Lines 1–8. A "bark" is a ship; sailors measured a star's height to find their way. Spelling as in the Project Gutenberg text.

full.title: Scanning a line
full.q: Mark the stresses in: "So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,"
steps: Say it aloud: so LONG as MEN can BREATHE or EYES can SEE.
Count: 10 syllables, 5 stresses, each weak syllable followed by a strong one.
That is five iambs: iambic pentameter.

full.html: Reading every sonnet as a true diary. The sonnets may draw on real feelings, but they are also artful performances in a fashionable form. We do not know how much is autobiography.

deep.html: Time is the great villain of the sonnets: his "bending sickle" mows down beauty and youth. Against him the poet sets three defenses: children (1–17), love itself (116), and poetry (18, 55, 60, 65). Following that thread through the sequence is a good way to read it.

items: Can words really outlast time? What else lasts?
Is true love really unchanging, as Sonnet 116 says? What would change your mind?
Why might a strict form like the sonnet help a poet rather than limit him?

deep.html: Petrarch and Dante (earlier on this ladder) wrote love poems that shaped the sonnet. Milton, later, wrote sonnets on politics and faith, proving the form could hold any subject.

questions: Sonnet 18 says the poem will keep its subject alive forever. Has it? Who is the poem's subject?
Sonnet 116 says love "alters not." Do you agree that real love does not change?
Why do you think poets like strict rules, like fourteen lines and a set rhyme?
If you could make one thing last forever by writing about it, what would you choose?
